subject: Very large fit objects in RStan

messages.author: a8b6459b77c849fe
messages.subject: Very large fit objects in RStan
parts:
I am mystified by the size of fit objects in RStan. I just ran a model that had 23,000 data points and included an "ll" vector in transformed parameters to save the log likelihoods for a WAIC calculation. With 4 chains and 1000 sampling iterations and 8 bytes per value, that comes to 697 MB. The fit object, saved to disk, is much larger than that -- it is 3.9 GB. When I extract the samples from the fit object, I can verify (with object.size) that the sample size is what I expect. Even if the fit object is storing all the warmup samples too, that still leaves 2.5 GB unaccounted for. I'm having a hard time seeing how everything else a fit object might contain would add up to even a fraction of the size of the sample. (BTW, the data itself is less than 1 MB).

Can anyone offer some insight on this?

messages.author: 1ccdd74b089d873c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Very large fit objects in RStan
parts:
I'd guess it's related to the .MISC slot of the stanfit object.  My understanding is that it's an environment meant to hold the results of calculations of summary statistics, etc., so that they only need to be calculated once.  The environment is created in the sampling method of stanmodel:

sfmiscenv <- new.env()

However, the default arguments of new.env (that is, parent = parent.frame() ) make the enclosing environment the environment associated with the evaluation of the sampling method, so when you save the fit object, you're also storing everything in that frame, which probably amounts to at least an additional copy of the samples and the data.

What's helped me in the past is to do something like the following manipulation of .MISC

stanfit <- stan("model.stan", ...)
stanfit@.MISC <- emptyenv()
save(stanfit, file = "savefile.RData")
## New session
load("savefile.Rdata")
stanfit@.MISC <- new.env(parent = globalenv())

Now .MISC doesn't have the same enclosing environment as it originally had, and if I try to get the summary again it will need to be recalculated, but I didn't notice any problems with that.  

A potential change to make the above workaround unnecessary would be to modify the source line above with sfmiscenv to specify a different enclosing environment ( globalenv() or emptyenv() )

Related from the serialization section of R internals manual:
 
Serialization in R needs to take into account that objects may contain references to environments, which then have enclosing environments and so on. (Environments recognized as package or name space environments are saved by name.) There are ‘reference objects’ which are not duplicated on copy and should remain shared on unserialization. These are weak references, external pointers and environments other than those associated with packages, namespaces and the global environment. These are handled via a hash table, and references after the first are written out as a reference marker indexed by the table entry.

Environments are treated in several ways: as we have seen, some are written as specific pseudo-SEXPTYPEs. Package and namespace environments are written with pseudo-SEXPTYPEs followed by the name. ‘Normal’ environments are written out as ENVSXPs with an integer indicating if the environment is locked followed by the enclosure, frame, ‘tag’ (the hash table) and attributes.  

See also: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/13912867/empty-r-environment-becomes-large-file-when-saved

> Related from the serialization section of R internals manual:
>
> Serialization in R needs to take into account that objects may contain references to environments, which then have enclosing environments and so on. (Environments recognized as package or name space environments are saved by name.) There are ‘reference objects’ which are not duplicated on copy and should remain shared on unserialization. These are weak references, external pointers and environments other than those associated with packages, namespaces and the global environment. These are handled via a hash table, and references after the first are written out as a reference marker indexed by the table entry.
>
> Environments are treated in several ways: as we have seen, some are written as specific pseudo-SEXPTYPEs. Package and namespace environments are written with pseudo-SEXPTYPEs followed by the name. ‘Normal’ environments are written out as ENVSXPs with an integer indicating if the environment is locked followed by the enclosure, frame, ‘tag’ (the hash table) and attributes.
>
> See also: http://stackoverflow.com/questions/13912867/empty-r-environment-becomes-large-file-when-saved
